title: Four Chariots and a Crown for the Branch
summary: In the eighth and final vision four chariots with teams of different colored horses come out from between two bronze mountains and go out to patrol the earth, and those sent to the north set God's Spirit at rest there. Then, in a sign-act, Zechariah is told to take silver and gold from exiles newly arrived from Babylon, make a crown, and set it on the head of Joshua the high priest, announcing a man called the Branch who will build the temple, rule on his throne, and serve as priest.
story: The visions began with horsemen patrolling the earth (1:7-17) and they end with chariots doing the same. In the first vision the world was at rest while Jerusalem lay in ruins; now God's forces have gone out and his Spirit is at rest in the north, the direction from which Judah's enemies and exile came. The series is complete: God has judged the nations, cleansed his leaders and his land, and set his purposes in motion. The chapter then closes the first major section of the book (1:7-6:15) not with another vision but with an action in the real world, a crown made and set on a head, pointing to the coming Branch who will build the temple and unite the roles of king and priest.
historical:
The exiles named in verse 10, Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah, had recently arrived from Babylon, perhaps bringing gifts for the temple, as later returnees did (Ezra 8:25-30). Josiah son of Zephaniah, at whose house they were staying, is otherwise unknown. In verse 14 Heldai is called Helem and Josiah apparently Hen, which the BSB takes as the gracious son of Zephaniah; the names vary in the Hebrew text, a common feature of ancient copying.

The crowning is historically puzzling. Joshua was the high priest, and in Judah's tradition the crown belonged to the king of David's line, which in 519 BC meant Zerubbabel. Crowning Zerubbabel as king would have looked like rebellion against Persia, which had just crushed revolts across the empire. Some scholars think the text originally named Zerubbabel and was later changed when his hopes faded, but there is no manuscript evidence for this. Others take the crown as placed on Joshua as a sign pointing beyond him to the Branch, and then kept in the temple as a memorial (verse 14), waiting for the one it was really for.
cultural:
The chariot was the most powerful weapon of the ancient Near East, the equivalent of the tank, and the Persian king's army and messengers used horse and chariot to control a vast empire. Bronze mountains may suggest the gate of heaven, God's dwelling place, from which his forces go out; in Mesopotamian art the sun god was sometimes pictured rising between two mountains, and Zechariah's image may borrow from that world while giving it a new meaning. The four chariots, like the four horns of chapter 1, point to the four directions and so to the whole earth; the Hebrew word for the four spirits in verse 5 can also mean the four winds.

Crowns were made of precious metal and could be layered; the Hebrew word here is plural, crowns, which may mean a crown of several rings or two crowns. In the ancient world gifts to a temple were often kept there as memorials to the donors, and the crown's placement in the temple as a memorial to the men who gave it follows that practice.
literary: The chapter has two parts that close the first half of the book. Verses 1-8 are the last of the eight night visions, mirroring the first with horses of various colors. The directions in verse 6 are hard to follow in Hebrew: the red horses are not given a direction, and toward the west translates a phrase that literally means after them. Verses 9-15 shift from vision to a prophetic sign-act, an action that acts out the message, like Jeremiah's yoke or Ezekiel's model of the siege. The oracle in verses 12-13 is built on repetition: the Branch will build the temple of the LORD, and the phrase is said twice, with a list of royal and priestly roles following.

outline.t: Eighth vision: four chariots go out over the earth
Silver and gold from the exiles and a crown for Joshua
The man called the Branch, priest and king
The crown as a memorial; those far away will build

doctrines.note: The four chariots go out at God's command from his dwelling to the ends of the earth. The nations that seemed to act freely are under the patrol of heaven, and God's purposes for his people are carried out by his own forces.

The Branch will build the temple, bear royal splendor, rule on his throne, and be a priest on his throne. The Old Testament usually kept king and priest separate; here they are brought together in one coming figure.
Those far away will come and help build the temple of the LORD (verse 15). The work of God's house is not limited to those already in Jerusalem; it will draw in people from afar.

words.note: Tsemach, Branch. The title from 3:8 returns, now with a play on words: a man whose name is the Branch, and he will branch out (literally, sprout) from his place. The image is of a living shoot growing up from what seemed a dead stump of David's family.

Atarah, crown. It is used for royal crowns (2 Samuel 12:30) and festive garlands. The form here is plural, which may describe an ornate crown of several bands. Placing it on the high priest's head was unusual, since priests wore a turban, not a crown.

Etsah, counsel or plan. The phrase peaceful counsel between the two in verse 13 describes harmony between the royal and priestly roles. Readers differ on whether the two are two people (a king and a priest working together) or two offices joined in one person.

Merkavah, chariot. The word is used for war chariots and royal chariots, and later Jewish mysticism used it for the throne-chariot of God seen by Ezekiel. Here the chariots carry God's rule to every direction of the earth.

christ: The New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom kingship and priesthood finally meet. Hebrews builds on Psalm 110, where the Messiah is both king and a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek, and it says that we have a high priest who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven (Hebrews 8:1). That is exactly the combination this chapter announces: a priest on his throne. The Branch who builds the temple of the LORD is taken up in Jesus's claim to raise up the temple of his body (John 2:19-21) and in the New Testament's picture of Christ building his church as God's dwelling (Matthew 16:18; Ephesians 2:20-22). The promise that those far away will come and build fits the gathering of Gentiles into that temple, since Paul calls them those who were once far away (Ephesians 2:13). Some interpreters also connect the four chariots with the four horsemen of Revelation 6, which draw on the same imagery.

hard.q: Why is the crown placed on Joshua the priest rather than on Zerubbabel, the heir of David?
hard.a: Several explanations are offered. Some scholars propose that the original text named Zerubbabel and was later changed to Joshua when Zerubbabel disappeared from history without becoming king; this is a conjecture without manuscript support. Others suggest that the plural crowns in verse 11 point to two crowns, one for each leader, though the text mentions only Joshua. Many interpreters hold that the text means what it says: Joshua is crowned as a sign, not as king. The oracle is addressed to him but speaks of another, a man whose name is the Branch, and the crown is then laid up in the temple for that coming one. On that reading, the crowning of a priest was a deliberate announcement that the future ruler would unite priesthood and kingship. Christians have seen the fulfillment in Christ, but on any reading the passage looks beyond the leaders of 519 BC.

questions: The first vision found the world at rest and Jerusalem forgotten; the last finds God's Spirit at rest after his work is done. How does it help you to know that God's timing is his own?
Why might it matter that the coming ruler is also a priest, one who both governs and intercedes?
The promise of verse 15 depends on diligent obedience. How do God's sure promises and his call to obey fit together in your own life?
